newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Last victim from Australia landslide recovered.
newsitem.headline: Last victim from Australia landslide recovered.

text.p: Rescuers on Thursday recovered the body of the last known victim from a landslide that killed 18 people a week ago, as the people of this Australian ski village began to rebuild their shattered lives.

There was only one survivor, ski instructor Stuart Diver, 27, who was trapped between slabs of broken concrete and was hauled to safety on Saturday after three nights in which he almost drowned in groundwater in freezing temperatures.
As news spread that the final body had been recovered from the rubble, the Thredbo Alpine Village, with a permanent population of barely 500, heaved a communal sigh of relief.

"I think the feeling...around the village is just one of relief that it is finally over," Thredbo Alpine Village managing director David Osborn told reporters. "They feel that the Thredbo community will survive and will go on."
The tiny ski resort plans to turn the massive landslide scar into a park with a memorial to the 18 dead, said Osborn.
"It will be a park forever more," he said. "I think that people started to get behind that and say that's a living breathing thing that can last forever more.
"The feeling that I get out of the community is the most appropriate thing is that it should just be a park."

Working in heavy rain on the scarred, unstable mountainside, in the Snowy Mountains south of Sydney, exhausted rescuers unearthed the 18th body from the hopelessly compacted rubble of two ski lodges at 2 a.m. (1600 GMT on Wednesday).
The landslide killed 11 men and seven women.
Diver's wife, Sally, was one of the 18 who died. They were in bed together when their lodge was engulfed near midnight on July 30 in a cascade of concrete, metal, trees, dirt and rocks.
But police on Thursday continued the grim task of removing the personal effects of those killed from the wreckage.
Police called the search and rescue effort a success, saying it had been too much to hope for another survivor as fortunate and mentally tough as Diver.
"It was a massive bonus," police superintendent Eric Gollan said of Diver's miraculous escape. "It was only professionalism that got that person out as a survivor."
Rescuers who had picked their way through the unstable slope for seven days are now preparing to clear the disaster scene with heavy machinery, but are being hampered by rain.
"We are reasonably confident we have explored any cavities that are there. It was just an absolute miracle that that cavity (where Diver lay trapped for three days) formed," Gollan said.

Police superintendent Charlie Sanderson, who has coordinated much of the rescue effort since the disaster, called the landslide a horrific tragedy that had touched every rescuer, especially those with the grisly task of retrieving bodies.
"The whole thing has been a really emotional experience for us," he told reporters. "I can tell you, up there (on the slope) today, there are people walking around hugging each other..."
Firefighter Paul Rugg described the wet, treacherous conditions they toiled under in the final hours of the search. "It was like a skating rink or standing on oil," he said.
